promptText: Some argue that raising the minimum wage cuts poverty and strengthens the economy. Others believe it drives businesses to raise prices and shed jobs. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The economic consequences of statutory increases to the wage floor.
distractors: The most effective means of reducing inequality across the whole economy.
The regulation of pay in low-margin and labour-intensive industries.
The distribution of income between employers and their own employees.

phases.correct: The alleviation of poverty and stimulation of demand through higher pay.
distractors: The elimination of household poverty through a single statutory measure.
The reduction of public expenditure on benefits paid to low-earning workers.
The improvement in morale and retention at better-paying firms.

phases.correct: transferring income to households that spend it locally, reducing reliance on state subsidy
distractors: guaranteeing that no household in work falls below the poverty line at any point
compelling profitable employers to distribute a larger share of their revenue to their lowest-paid staff
narrowing the gap between the lowest and the median earnings in a country

phases.correct: Jurisdictions where phased increases raised incomes without measurable job loss.
distractors: Countries that abolished poverty entirely after legislating a wage floor.
Cities that pledged a living wage for all municipal staff within the decade.
Firms that raised pay voluntarily and recorded higher productivity.

phases.correct: the gain holds only while the increase remains proportionate to local productivity
distractors: a statutory rise has never cost a single job in any economy that has ever attempted one
additional earnings are spent locally, sustaining the very businesses that pay them out
the public purse gains twice, through higher tax receipts and through lower benefit payments

phases.correct: The inflationary and employment-suppressing effect of mandated pay.
distractors: The inevitability of redundancies wherever any wage floor is imposed at all.
The vulnerability of small firms operating upon very narrow margins.
The acceleration of automation in low-paid occupations.

phases.correct: raising the cost of labour above its productive value, prompting cuts to hours
distractors: confronting small firms operating upon very narrow margins with an unaffordable bill
transferring income to households that spend it in local shops and services
replacing the counter staff of a high-street cafe with a self-service screen

phases.correct: Labour-intensive sectors cutting rostered hours and adopting self-service.
distractors: Firms pledging to keep every employee whatever the wage floor becomes.
Trade bodies warning that any increase will force every member to shut.
Small retailers raising prices after a rise in the cost of stock.

phases.correct: employers in concentrated markets set wages, so moderate floors need not displace labour
distractors: no employer anywhere has ever absorbed a statutory increase without reducing the hours it rosters
labour-intensive firms habitually answer a higher wage bill by reducing the hours that they roster
the gain to households evaporates where prices rise faster than the statutory floor itself

phases.correct: the floor should be set by independent assessment of regional productivity
distractors: the wage floor should be raised continuously until poverty has been eliminated altogether
the floor should be frozen at its present level until the economy has fully recovered
the state should top up low pay through tax credits rather than legislate

phases.correct: the outcome turns upon calibration to local conditions rather than upon the policy itself
distractors: the state should determine the pay of every worker rather than leave it to the market
poverty among working households cannot be relieved by higher wages alone
the minimum wage should be set by an independent body with reference to regional productivity

promptText: All children should study a foreign language in school, starting in the earliest grades. To what extent do you agree or disagree with this statement?

phases.correct: The mandating of foreign language acquisition in early childhood education.
distractors: The place of foreign language teaching in adult and vocational education.
The techniques best suited to teaching vocabulary to young children.
The ascendancy of English as the world's principal language of exchange.

phases.correct: The necessity of preserving foundational native language skills.
distractors: The impossibility of acquiring two languages at once in early childhood.
The comparative difficulty of mastering two grammatical systems simultaneously.
The single weekly period allotted to a foreign language in many primary schools.

phases.correct: ensuring young learners establish robust cognitive frameworks in a single language before additional systems are layered upon them
distractors: consolidating mother-tongue literacy completely before any second grammatical system is introduced into the classroom
ensuring that every pupil leaves primary school reading and writing the mother tongue to a flawless standard
allowing class teachers to devote the entire language timetable to a single subject rather than dividing it between two competing ones

phases.correct: Educational models that delay intensive foreign language instruction until native literacy benchmarks are secured.
distractors: Adult education institutes that require candidates to demonstrate full literacy before enrolling upon a language course.
Primary schools that allocate no more than one short weekly period to foreign language study.
Kindergartens in which songs, stories and games are conducted entirely in a second language.

phases.correct: postponing bilingualism forfeits the period of highest natural phonetic absorption, which cannot be recovered later
distractors: adults who study a language after retirement show some protection against cognitive decline
early programmes taught by non-specialists can leave pupils with poor pronunciation to unlearn
children who read fluently in one language transfer that skill readily to any later one

phases.correct: The exploitation of the critical window of childhood neuroplasticity.
distractors: The effortlessness with which any child whatsoever masters any language at all.
The labour-market advantage conferred upon adults by early bilingualism.
The cultural curiosity awakened in a child by contact with another language.

phases.correct: capitalising on the brain's innate capacity for effortless phonological and grammatical acquisition before it diminishes
distractors: conducting kindergarten songs, stories and games entirely in the target language so that exposure is constant throughout the day
awakening in young pupils an enduring interest in foreign countries and unfamiliar cultural practices
placing trained native speakers in primary classrooms so that pronunciation is modelled from the outset

phases.correct: Bilingual immersion programmes in which infants acquire a second language through ordinary play and instruction.
distractors: Secondary schools in which trained native speakers model pronunciation from the first year of language study.
Ministerial promises that every primary pupil will study a second language within five years.
Expatriate families whose children acquire complete fluency merely by attending an ordinary neighbourhood school.

phases.correct: poorly designed early language programmes can induce academic anxiety and produce superficial competence in both languages
distractors: no primary school anywhere possesses staff able to teach the target language to a native standard
young children acquire the sounds of a new language with an accuracy that adults rarely match
pupils who begin a language only at secondary school seldom reach comfortable fluency

phases.correct: early play-based immersion should begin in the first grades while intensive native literacy is safeguarded
distractors: every child in the world should begin a second language in the first year of school regardless of the resources available
children ought to secure complete literacy in the mother tongue first, with a second language introduced systematically only upon entry to secondary school
the decision as to when a child begins a second language properly belongs to the individual family rather than to the state

phases.correct: optimal cognitive development requires the neurological benefits of early bilingualism without sacrificing the grounding of a mother tongue
distractors: the economic advantage conferred by bilingualism is felt chiefly by adults competing within an international labour market
a globalised labour market consistently rewards those able to operate confidently in more than one language from an early age
young children absorb unfamiliar languages far more rapidly than adolescents, and the advantage conferred by that facility is irrecoverable once lost

promptText: Children today spend more time watching television than they did in the past. Describe some of the advantages and disadvantages of television for children.

phases.correct: The effects of increased television viewing upon children.
distractors: The rising consumption of streaming and social media by adult audiences.
The techniques broadcasters use to retain a young viewer's attention.
The decline in the time children devote to reading.

phases.correct: The educational potential of high-quality programming for young viewers.
distractors: The capacity of television to replace formal schooling entirely.
The reinforcement of classroom lessons through repetition.
The suitability of programmes designed for a young audience.

phases.correct: democratising access to global knowledge and diverse cultural narratives
distractors: holding a child's attention through rapid editing, bright colour and repetitive jingles
sustaining a child's attention for long stretches without adult supervision
guaranteeing that every young viewer leaves the screen measurably better informed

phases.correct: Natural history and science documentaries watched by children at home each evening.
distractors: Televised lecture courses that universities broadcast to adult learners in remote regions.
Broadcasters' promises that every children's programme will carry educational value.
Classroom screenings of documentary films at the end of the school week.

phases.correct: this passive consumption inherently limits active physical engagement and real-world problem-solving
distractors: no child has ever acquired from any broadcast a single piece of knowledge that endures beyond the programme itself
the harm attributed to the screen depends largely on how long and how late a child watches
children who watch documentaries regularly arrive at school with wider vocabularies

phases.correct: The detrimental impact of prolonged viewing on physical and social development.
distractors: The hours of vigorous outdoor play that the screen has replaced.
The reliance of parents upon the screen as a substitute carer.
The strain that prolonged viewing places upon eyesight and sleep.

phases.correct: catalysing sedentary behaviours and reducing organic interpersonal communication
distractors: rendering children who watch television inactive, uncommunicative and physically unfit
exposing young viewers to advertising for toys and sugary foods during each break
abolishing conversation of any kind from the household in which a set is switched on

phases.correct: Rising rates of childhood obesity and delayed social skills in highly digitised households.
distractors: Children confined indoors for the hours that an earlier generation spent in vigorous play.
Pupils arriving at school able to recount in detail a documentary they watched the previous evening.
Parental resolutions to limit viewing that are abandoned within a week.

phases.correct: television is merely a tool, and these harms stem largely from absent parental mediation rather than from the medium itself
distractors: a child raised without any television at all will invariably develop stronger social and physical capacities
the hours a child spends before a screen are hours withheld from the vigorous play that a growing body requires
contemporary children's programming is so saturated with advertising that no single episode passes without some form of commercial persuasion

phases.correct: the educational potential of television is real, but it must be managed through strict parental oversight to mitigate the risks of unregulated, sedentary screen time
distractors: children should be forbidden any screen whatever until adolescence, since no programme can offer what active outdoor play provides
daily viewing ought to be capped at a single hour on school nights and left entirely to the family's discretion at weekends and in the holidays
the television set should be removed from the family home altogether so that children turn instead to reading and to active play

phases.correct: optimal human development requires a balance between rapid digital cognitive stimulation and essential physical and social maturation
distractors: the influence of any medium upon the population at large is determined entirely by the regulation that the state imposes upon its broadcasters
no programme, however carefully it is made, can offer a child anything that an afternoon of active outdoor play does not offer far better
parents should permit high-quality educational viewing while enforcing firm daily limits upon the total hours a child spends before the screen

promptText: Everybody should be allowed admission to university or college programs regardless of their level of academic ability. To what extent do you agree or disagree with this statement?

phases.correct: The democratisation of admission to tertiary education programmes.
distractors: The widening of access to schooling at every level of the education system.
The value of a degree in an increasingly crowded labour market.
The expansion of university places in developing nations.

phases.correct: The necessity of preserving elite academic standards at degree level.
distractors: The impossibility of teaching any degree to an unselected cohort.
The fairness of competitive examination as a selection device.
The limited number of places available on specialised and expensive courses.

phases.correct: ensuring that specialised programmes are populated exclusively by cohorts capable of handling rigorous, advanced-level coursework
distractors: reserving every place in the education system from secondary school upwards for those with the highest results
restricting cohort numbers so that teaching staff are able to supervise the progress of each student individually
obliging every candidate to sit a standardised national entrance examination before any offer of a place is issued

phases.correct: Highly selective admissions processes at top-tier research institutions.
distractors: Programmes populated exclusively by cohorts able to manage advanced coursework.
Faculties that reserve a share of their places for applicants from poor districts.
University pledges to admit only the most able applicants from every school in the country.

phases.correct: rigid enforcement of this perspective perpetuates socioeconomic disparities, since early academic performance is closely tied to financial privilege
distractors: no examination taken at eighteen has ever predicted anything whatever about a candidate's capacity for sustained degree study
competitive admission ensures that demanding degree programmes are populated by candidates genuinely able to complete them
an institution that admits every applicant regardless of preparation will see a substantial proportion of them withdraw before the end of the first year

phases.correct: The dismantling of systemic socioeconomic barriers to entry.
distractors: The right of every citizen to schooling of any kind at public expense.
The contribution of graduates to national economic growth.
The provision of second chances for mature applicants.

phases.correct: facilitating upward social mobility and equitable access to specialised knowledge
distractors: admitting mature applicants who hold no formal qualification of any kind
ensuring that every citizen eventually holds a university degree
enlarging the pool of qualified graduates upon which an economy can draw

phases.correct: The widespread success of open-enrolment community college systems in North America.
distractors: Secondary schools that accept every child in their catchment area without any selection.
State scholarships awarded to the undergraduates with the highest marks in the national examination.
Government targets for the proportion of undergraduates drawn from disadvantaged schools within a decade.

phases.correct: unmitigated adherence to this model often triggers the dilution of academic rigour and the overextension of university resources
distractors: an institution that admits students without any selection will invariably see its academic standards collapse within a single generation
open enrolment offers a second opportunity to those applicants whose secondary schooling had failed them at eighteen
school results at eighteen reflect the quality of the school attended as much as the ability of the pupil

phases.correct: policymakers must leverage the accessibility of open enrolment for foundational programmes while deploying rigorous standards for advanced research institutions
distractors: every applicant should be admitted to any programme they choose, since no institution is entitled to judge a candidate's potential in advance
entry requirements should be relaxed substantially for applicants from disadvantaged backgrounds while remaining wholly unchanged for every other category of applicant
admission should be made universal, with tuition fees calibrated according to the grades an applicant has obtained at secondary school

phases.correct: a sustainable and equitable education system must balance broad societal uplift with the preservation of cutting-edge academic excellence
distractors: a nation's prosperity depends upon the proportion of its whole population that has completed some form of schooling
a modern economy depends upon producing the largest possible number of well-qualified and adaptable graduates each year
opportunity denied at eighteen is rarely recovered, and the cost of that exclusion falls upon the whole community
